I was bullied out of nursing school in 2016, and one of the hardest parts was feeling like some of the people in authority wanted to minimize it or act like it never really happened.

Years later, the same school offered to let me pick up where I left off, but I chose to start the program over from the beginning. I came back, finished in 2025, and graduated with a 4.0.

What surprised me most was that the academics were never the hardest part. The harder part was rebuilding my confidence and learning not to let other people decide whether I belonged in nursing.

Nursing school should be challenging, but bullying, humiliation, and “eating our young” should never be normalized as part of becoming a nurse.

Looking back, I’m just grateful I came back and finished what I started.

My mother became an RN in the early 70's and retired in 2017.

She worked all over the US in both rural and urban settings. 

She said a lot changed from when she started to when she retired. 

Instead of 8 hour shifts it was changed to 12 hour shifts, then they decided LPN's weren't needed, then no CNA's. She went from being allowed a maximum of 4 patients per nurse to sometimes having as many as 7 or 8, ICU went from 1 to 1 to up to 3 patients per nurse. (A bit hard to parse because historically nursing was a bit more cooperative/overlapping/sharing patient responsibilities)

By the time my mother retired they had one RN doing what previously required 3 staff.
